definition: In computer science, incremental learning is a method of machine learning in which input data is continuously used to extend the existing model's knowledge i.e.
details: to further train the model. It represents a dynamic technique of supervised learning and unsupervised learning that can be applied when training data becomes available gradually over time or its size is out of system memory limits. Algorithms that can facilitate incremental learning are known as incremental machine learning algorithms. In contemporary machine learning literature, settings that require learning from a sequence of tasks while limiting catastrophic forgetting are often discussed under the closely related term continual learning. Many traditional machine learning algorithms inherently support incremental learning. Other algorithms can be adapted to facilitate incremental learning. Examples of incremental algorithms include decision trees (IDE4, ID5R and gaenari), decision rules, artificial neural networks (RBF networks, Learn++, Fuzzy ARTMAP, TopoART, and IGNG) or the incremental SVM. The aim of incremental learning is for the learning model to adapt to new data without forgetting its existing knowledge. Some incremental learners have built-in some parameter or assumption that controls the relevancy of old data, while others, called stable incremental machine learning

explainer.lead: Incremental learning is machine learning that continuously uses incoming data to extend an existing model's knowledge by further training it. It matters when data arrives gradually over time or is too large to fit in system memory.

tiers.eli5: It's like adding new words to a notebook you already keep, rather than starting a fresh notebook every time you learn something.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to update models as new data streams in, under both supervised and unsupervised settings. A pitfall is catastrophic forgetting, where learning new material erases earlier knowledge; limiting this is a central concern in the literature.
tiers.paperLevel: A dynamic learning technique in which the model is further trained on continuously supplied data rather than retrained from scratch. Formal study often frames it as learning from a sequence of tasks under bounded catastrophic forgetting.

explainer.example: A model trained on a batch of data is later further trained on newly collected samples, extending its knowledge without a full rebuild.
